newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf Oil Outlook - Sellers seek floor.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf Oil Outlook - Sellers seek floor.

text.p: Badly-dented middle distillate prices and premiums are expected to hit a floor and stage a modest but possibly short-lived recovery in the coming week if Indian subcontinent interest returns and the Mediterranean arbitrage remains shut, Mideast Gulf traders said Thursday.

With Gulf gas oil and kerosene prices at 12-month lows, market premia for end June cargoes evaporating and Singapore flooded with supply the outlook for sellers remained difficult but not entirely lost, they said.
"Term lifters have taken a serious hit for sure but for July the market is looking partly rosy," said one regional trader.
Gulf gas oil talked around $21.50 a barrel fob on Thursday and end June cargoes without a home in India appeared to trade at a slight discount to the quote for the first time this year.
Gas oil from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain commanded a $1.00 premium to independent price quotes in early June 1996.
But with the arbitrage from the Mediterranean closed and demand from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh said steady, late July sellers still hung on for plus-30 cents.
"Even for July 1-10 cargoes it's brighter...That's why there's a wide bid-ask spread," said a trader, adding that market quotes ran from minus 10 cents to plus 30 cents.

Steadier naphtha and fuel oil markets and expectations of higher diesel burning to satisfy increased air conditioning demand as the Gulf entered summer also offered some comfort to middle distillate sellers, traders said.
India Oil Corp's (IOC) denial on Wednesday of a newspaper report that it had exhausted an enhanced $3.5 billion external commercial borrowing (ECB) limit was also said supportive.
"It dispelled some fears that IOC would have to temporarily slow down its (crude oil and refined products) imports," said one trader in the Gulf.
Gulf naphtha markets were lower in line with crude losses though fundamentals pointed to resilient short-term prices of $180-$190 a tonne and a premium of $10 over quotes.
Term naphtha talks involving Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) and Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) with their term lifters for supplies from July and August respectively continue.
ADNOC had targeted a premium of $22.50 over the premium, up from $6.80 while KPC sought $20, up from $7.90 justifying the hike by pointing to higher petrochemical demand, traders said.
Fuel oil markets in the Gulf have also rode out the storm of falling crude markets in a better shape than middle distillates with 380-cst bunkers at Fujairah flat at $95-97 a tonne.
Spot market discounts to quotes held at minus $3/5.
